newsitem.title: UK: Hard-hitting treatment helps arthritis - studies.
newsitem.headline: Hard-hitting treatment helps arthritis - studies.

text.p: Two teams of researchers into rheumatoid arthritis published reports on Friday that indicate hard-hitting treatment may work better than the usual gradual approach to the crippling disease.

Dutch and Belgian doctors said a strong drug cocktail helped stop the disease from damaging patients' bodies when given early, while an Australian specialist resorted to a bone-marrow transplant in another patient and reported near-miraculous results.
Rheumatoid arthritis is an auto-immune disease, caused by the body's immune system for some reason turning against the tissue in the joints.

D.J.L.Joske of Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital in Nedlands, Western Australia, tried a bone marrow transplant -- used to restore seriously suppressed immune systems -- in a 46-year-old man so crippled he could not walk.
The transplant worked.
"From being virtually bound to his wheelchair, he was able to walk two 2 km (1.2 miles) easily," Joske wrote in a letter to the medical journal the Lancet.
Although such transplants are very risky, Joske said they may be worth it for such severely debilitated patients.
He was not sure why the transplant worked, but assumed the immune system was somehow "re-set" to its normal mode.
Such extreme treatment could never become standard for rheumatoid arthritis, which affects millions around the world. But researchers suggest a gentle approach may not be the best.

Dr Maarten Boers of Free University Hospital in Amsterdam and colleagues across Belgium and the Netherlands decided to test the traditional approach that gradually phases in stronger drugs for the crippling illness.

They treated 155 volunteers with early rheumatoid arthritis. Half received standard treatment with sulphasalazine, a second-line drug that is used when non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen do not work.
The other half got a combination of the powerful steroid prednisolone and the immune suppressant methotrexate, which are usually considered "third-line" drugs for the toughest cases.
They then phased out the strong drugs and treated the patients with sulphasalazine alone.

Reporting in the Lancet, Boers's group said the pain, inflammation and other crippling effects of the rheumatoid arthritis were suppressed in 72 percent of the group treated with the strong combination.
Forty-nine percent of the sulphasalazine group saw their symptoms suppressed.
The inflammation that marks rheumatoid arthritis causes permanent damage, including the erosion of cartilage and bone, so treating the symptoms is important.
"This approach may prove useful in the treatment of early rheumatoid arthritis," Boers's group wrote.
But after 80 weeks both groups reverted to the same degree of symptoms.
Paul Emery, an expert at the University of Leeds, said the study had important conclusions.
"The first is that, if inflammation is suppressed, patients gain predictable benefit for the duration of that suppression," he wrote in a commentary on Boers's paper.
"Next, more therapy is not necessarily more toxic.
"Finally, the therapy did not fundamentally affect the underlying disease process."
Emery said obviously a cure would be better but none was in sight.
"For the present, the message is clear: suppression of rheumatoid arthritis is feasible and effective but a cure is some way off."
